claims.claim: A 2017 Management Science paper, accepted by Uri Gneezy, compared prediction markets and prediction polls with more than 2,400 participants forecasting 261 events over two seasons of a geopolitical tournament.
claims.episode_span: More than 2,400 people forecast 261 events across two seasons of a geopolitical prediction tournament
claims.source_title: Distilling the Wisdom of Crowds: Prediction Markets vs. Prediction Polls
claims.supporting_quote: More than 2,400 participants made forecasts on 261 events over two seasons of a geopolitical prediction tournament.

claims.claim: In both seasons, prediction-market prices were more accurate than the simple mean of prediction-poll forecasts, but aggregated team polls outperformed markets.
claims.episode_span: Market prices were more accurate than the simple average of poll forecasts in both seasons.
claims.source_title: Distilling the Wisdom of Crowds: Prediction Markets vs. Prediction Polls
claims.supporting_quote: In both seasons of the tournament, prices from the prediction market were more accurate than the simple mean of forecasts from prediction polls.

claims.claim: Team prediction polls beat markets when aggregated with temporal decay, past-performance weighting, and recalibration, with the biggest poll advantage at the start of long-duration questions.
claims.episode_span: Team polls then beat the markets, but only after the forecasts were combined with temporal decay, more weight for forecasters who had done well before, and recalibration.
claims.source_title: Distilling the Wisdom of Crowds: Prediction Markets vs. Prediction Polls
claims.supporting_quote: However, team prediction polls outperformed prediction markets when forecasts were statistically aggregated using temporal decay, differential weighting based on past performance, and recalibration.
